items.title: About stroke consistency
items.body: General information, not a finding about your swimming. A review of swimming coordination argues that there is no single ideal coordination pattern that every swimmer should copy: skilled swimming balances a stable pattern with variation that adapts to the swimmer, the task and the conditions. (Seifert et al., 2014) Elite swimmers showed less variation of hip speed within the stroke cycle than recreational swimmers, and kept it stable across paces, while it rose with pace in the recreational group. (Schnitzler et al., 2010) What AquaTrack can look at today: From a side-view clip AquaTrack times each stroke cycle and reports how much the cycle time varies. With six or more cycles of one arm it can point to the cycles that were off your own rhythm. What it cannot: It cannot measure how your speed changes inside each stroke, which is what the research on steadiness and skill level measured.
limitations: A theoretical review, not a test of any threshold.
Does not say how much variation in cycle time is useful or harmful.
A different kind of steadiness from cycle-to-cycle timing.

items.title: Stroke rate, Time per stroke cycle, Stroke cycles counted, Rhythm variation, Body line angle, Legs against the trunk line, Head against the trunk line, Pull depth, Elbow bend in the pull (2D), Pull path variation, Cycle time, start to end
items.body: The swimmer could not be followed reliably enough in this clip. What would help: A side-view clip in which the swimmer stays fully visible for at least six strokes of one arm.

items.title: Left-right balance
items.body: Needs both arms followed through whole pulls. From the side the far arm is hidden behind the body for part of every pull.

items.title: Arm coordination
items.body: Needs the start and end of both arms' pulls. The far arm's are hidden from a side view.

items.title: Kick rhythm
items.body: Kick beats are computed but have not been checked against video yet, and the far leg is often hidden.

items.title: Breathing timing
items.body: The head turn is not seen reliably from an underwater side view; the experimental detector has not been checked against video.

items.title: Body rotation
items.body: Rotation around the body's long axis cannot be measured from one side camera. It needs a front or overhead view.

items.title: Propulsion and efficiency
items.body: Force and efficiency cannot be measured from video of joint positions alone.

items.title: Change since earlier swims
items.body: This is a baseline: there is no earlier swim that can be compared with it. What would help: Another clip of the same distance and effort, filmed the same way.

items.title: Whether any value is good or bad
items.body: No reference values have been verified for these measurements, so nothing is compared with other swimmers or with an ideal.

checkpoints.title: Film side-on with a steady view
checkpoints.what_to_film: Under water from the side, the camera level and either moving along with you or held still. Keep your whole body in the picture.
checkpoints.minimum: At least 6 full cycles of one arm.
limitations: Better footage makes more measurable; it does not guarantee that every measurement will pass its checks.

references.citation: Seifert L, et al. (2014). Coordination Pattern Variability Provides Functional Adaptations to Constraints in Swimming Performance. Sports Medicine 44(10):1333-1345.
references.population: Review of studies on inter-limb coordination in swimming

references.citation: Schnitzler C, et al. (2010). Hip Velocity and Arm Coordination in Front Crawl Swimming. International Journal of Sports Medicine 31(12):875-881.
references.population: 22 swimmers in an elite and a recreational group

recording_tips: Freestyle, filmed under water from the side, is what the analysis is built for.
Keep the whole swimmer in the picture, head to feet, for the whole clip.
Hold the camera level and side-on. Move it along with the swimmer or keep it still; avoid zooming, and avoid filming a swimmer who comes toward the camera or swims away from it.
Film at least six full strokes of one arm (about 8 to 15 seconds). Longer is better for rhythm.
Clear water and good light help; splashes, bubbles and other swimmers in front hide the body.
For comparing two swims, film the same distance at the same effort from the same place.
